newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: G10 central banks to collect derivatives data 1998.
newsitem.headline: G10 central banks to collect derivatives data 1998.

text.p: Leading central banks will start collecting data from big banks next year on the huge derivatives markets so they can better monitor the global financial system, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said Sunday.

The data on a broad range of foreign exchange, interest rate and equity derivatives will be gathered from mid-1998 from top dealers by national central banks in the Group of 10 leading industrial nations and then published by the BIS.

The aim is to present internationally consistent data on Over-The-Counter (OTC) instruments. The OTC market is several times the size of the exchange-traded market and largely unregulated because contracts are made between institutions.
Central bankers have often voiced concern about the rapid growth in OTC derivatives, but have lacked accurate data.
Finance ministers from the Group of Seven industrial nations called for improved reporting and disclosure of derivatives at the Lyon Summit last June.
G7 comprises the United States, Japan, Canada, Germany, Britain, Italy and France.
G10, which in fact is 11 countries, comprises the G7 plus the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Switzerland.
So far, the only reliable data on the OTC market have been from the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA), but these have not been comprehensive.

Although derivatives have exacerbated market volatility, central bankers have also stressed their role in strengthening the financial system by shifting risks to investors most willing and able to bear them.

"At the same time, it had become clear that improved information on the size and structure of derivatives markets is needed to increase market transparency and thereby help central banks, other authorities and market participants to better monitor patterns of activity in the global financial system," the BIS said in a statement.

Comprehensive data on derivatives should not only give central banks a better understanding of the financial sector -- including how derivatives affect the speed of market movements and how players respond to interest rate and exchange rate changes -- but also improve the transparency of markets.
The BIS, central bank to the worlds' central banks, will initially publish the global statistics every six months, but officials hope to increase the frequency.

The statistics, which will also include derivatives-related credit exposures before and after netting arrangements, will be based on consolidated reports by around 80 dealers worldwide to their national central banks and securities regulators.
The data will be based on the notional amounts and outstanding gross market values of a broad range of derivatives instruments on the books of institutions on June 30.
The reporting framework that central banks will use to collect the data is based on a July 1996 report from the Euro-currency Standing Committee, one of the BIS committees.
Following consultation with financial institutions and supervisors, the final framework that has been agreed by G10 reduces the reporting burden on institutions, the BIS said.
The first attempt at gathering comprehensive data on the OTC market was done in 1995 as part of BIS's triennial survey of foreign exchange and derivatives market activity.
The survey revealed much greater activity in derivative products than central bankers had previously been aware of.
The BIS's global survey, however, is only conducted every three years and is merely a snapshot of the market, hardly enough for central banks to be able to track developments.
The report, which was based on surveys in 26 countries, estimated the notional amount of OTC derivatives outstanding at end-March 1995 at $47.5 trillion.
Total reported gross market value, which gives some notion of credit risks, amounted to $2.2 trillion.
Global daily turnover in OTC foreign exchange and interest rate derivatives in April 1995 amounted to some $900 billion.
((-- Zurich Editorial 41 1 631 7340))
